extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; aspiring essayists, satirists, historians, and young professionals (e.g., lawyers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prescriptive observations for composing public essays and character sketches that argue moral points, satirize social types, and instruct or admonish readers; includes advice relevant to historians, speakers, and dramatists. Grounded in early-18th-century periodical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not interpret neighbours' misfortunes as divine punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be guilty of a greater Act of Uncharitableness, than to interpret the Afflictions which befal our Neighbours, as Punishments and Judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: treating misfortune as a judgment aggravates the sufferer's distress and diminishes compassion in others; it is presumptuous toward the divine. Examples/anti-patterns: the old maiden 'Nemesis' who finds a crime for every misfortune; historians who turn ill success into providential revelation. Use this principle as a moral and rhetorical restraint when explaining or narrating others' suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dressing superstition or folly in pompous style
rubrics_metrics.description: The very Description of this Folly, in ordinary Life, is sufficient to expose it; but when it appears in a Pomp and Dignity of Style, it is very apt to amuse and terrify the Mind of the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning for writers: elevated diction and majestic narrative can make absurd or superstitious claims seem venerable and persuasive. Do not rely on stately style to lend authority to unfounded causal claims (e.g., providential explanations); match style to the truth and soundness of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians should not claim insight into Providence
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Historians, as well Christian as Pagan, have fallen into this idle Superstition, and spoken of ill Success, unforeseen Disasters, and terrible Events, as if they had been let into the Secrets of Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive for historical writing: avoid presenting chance events or misfortunes as evidence of divine favour or wrath. Refrain from asserting knowledge of hidden providential designs; prefer probative, humane explanations over moralizing narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that calamities befall virtuous and wicked alike
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, there is no Calamity or Affliction, which is supposed to have happened as a Judgment to a vicious Man, which does not sometimes happen to Men of approved Religion and Virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this empirical check when arguing causation between vice and misfortune: because good and bad people both suffer, attributing a specific misfortune to a specific vice is unreliable. Example used: the sailors blaming Diagoras for a tempest — check for the broader distribution of events before asserting moral causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature judgments about whether events are blessings or calamities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for us to know what are Calamities, and what are Blessings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against rash moral or narrative verdicts made at an event's outset; many apparent misfortunes later prove advantageous (illustrated by the story of Biton and Clitobus). As a writer/critic, indicate uncertainty, follow consequences rather than the mere appearance of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentors should introduce modest but talented novices into practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Pliny...is very sollicitous in recommending to the Publick some young Men of his own Profession, and very often undertakes to become an Advocate, upon condition that some one of these his Favourites might be joined with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical professional guidance: patrons and established practitioners ought to create openings for modest, able beginners (e.g., let them observe, join cases, be introduced gradually). In rhetorical/formal genres, fostering talent includes providing opportunity to perform before audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance modesty with a manifest resolution to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty must be an Act of the Will, and yet it always implies Self-Denial... when a Man has an ardent Desire to do what is laudable... and, from an unmanly Bashfulness, shrinks away... he ought not to be angry at the World that a more unskilful Actor succeeds in his Part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for speakers and authors: modesty is virtuous but must be paired with deliberate self-assertion when appropriate; cultivate a 'latent resolution' so talent is not silenced by bashfulness. Avoid passive modesty that prevents contribution; training should encourage controlled readiness to present one’s ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate for eloquence and the ability to perform before great audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a ridiculous Education which does not qualify a Man to make his best Appearance before the greatest Man and the finest Woman to whom he can address himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical guideline: curricula (esp. in universities) should include practical training in public speaking and presence so that students can deploy their knowledge confidently in high-stakes encounters; failing this produces timid but learned persons who are outcompeted by blusterers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, seemingly insignificant details as dramatic plot catalysts
rubrics_metrics.description: Into what tragical Extravagancies does Shakespear hurry Othello upon the loss of an Handkerchief only?... what Barbarities does Desdemona suffer from a slight Inadvertency in regard to this fatal Trifle?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storytelling principle: minor objects or accidents can plausibly trigger major consequences — employ small details as credible engines of plot escalation. Beware also that trivialities can have outsized emotional or social effects; use them deliberately to create irony or tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray domestic minutiae for comic character effect
rubrics_metrics.description: He could preserve Apricots, and make Gellies... He has the whitest Hand that you ever saw... These Qualifications make him a sad Husband: He is perpetually in the Kitchin, and has a thousand Squabbles with the Cook-maid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for character sketching and satire: vivid, specific domestic details (culinary skills, household habits, petty quarrels) create comic contrast and make characters memorable. Specificity of small trades/skills heightens ridicule when they contradict social expectations (e.g., effeminate man in domestic role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invert gendered traits to produce satirical parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should not a Female Character be as ridiculous in a Man, as a Male Character in one of our Sex?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical strategy: apply traits stereotypically associated with one sex to the other to expose absurdities and double standards. Use inversion to make readers question normative roles and to produce ridicule on equal terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dreams as literary devices to suggest the soul's activity and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall consider this Subject in another Light, as Dreams may give us some Idea of the great Excellency of an Human Soul, and some Intimation of its Independency on Matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical/literary guidance: dream sequences can be used not merely as omens or revelations but to illustrate inner life and the soul's agency independent of the body. Employ dreams to dramatize psychological or metaphysical claims about character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting private bias as universal religious truth
rubrics_metrics.description: This Humour of turning every Misfortune into a Judgment, proceeds from wrong Notions of Religion, which, in its own nature, produces Goodwill towards Men, and puts the mildest Construction upon every Accident that befalls them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical rhetorical rule: do not let personal malice, envy, or gloomy temperament distort religious or moral language into instruments of judgement. Writers should frame religious claims as promoting compassion, and expose the appearance of opinion that arises from temperament rather than theology.
